y1-academic-career: Both develop academic learning, reflection and personal study direction. UCR also includes writing and civic engagement.
y1-computational-biology: Both develop mathematical descriptions and dynamic models of scientific processes. Leiden applies stochastic, discrete and continuous models in R to biology; UCR uses general calculus, differential equations and a model project in Mathematica.
y1-chemistry-life: Both study biomolecular structure and biochemical reactions. UCR emphasises enzymes and metabolism; Leiden also introduces general chemical concepts, acid–base reasoning and titration.
y1-basic-genetics: Both study inheritance and genetic variation. UCR applies these to human disease and genetic diagnosis rather than the maize phenotype experiment or full introductory chromosome-mapping sequence.
y1-lab-skills: Both develop hands-on laboratory formation, experimental technique, reproducible records and scientific reporting. UCR uses biochemical, microbial and molecular investigations rather than the identical introductory exercises.
y1-molecular-genetics: Both study DNA replication/repair, gene expression, cellular regulation and research approaches. Leiden additionally has a dedicated recombinant-DNA laboratory; UCR integrates molecular targets and cellular mechanisms.
y1-cell-biology: Both introduce cell structures, membranes, signalling, division and their molecular basis. The UCR course is a broader biomedical foundation.
y1-microbiology-immunobiology: Both study microbes, host defence, innate/adaptive immunity and immune mechanisms; UCR emphasises infection and immunopathology.
y1-statistics: Both develop probability and statistical inference for research. UCR emphasises mathematical statistics and simulation; Leiden additionally teaches practical R regression and reporting.
y1-animal-biodiversity: Both study animal diversity and classification. UCR surveys the whole tree of life, including plants and microorganisms, rather than reproducing the dedicated animal sequence.
y1-organismal-biology: Both study animal structure, function and regulation. UCR concentrates on adult human physiology and does not supply the plant component.
y1-behavioural-biology: Both examine animal behaviour and its biological mechanisms. UCR approaches these through comparative nervous-system anatomy, physiology, regulatory behaviour and research models.
y2-evolutionary-biology: Both develop evolutionary mechanisms, genetic variation, adaptation, speciation and evolutionary history; UCR does not reproduce every advanced Leiden application.
y2-population-community: Both study population dynamics, competition, predation, communities and biodiversity, with ecological modelling. UCR extends across ecosystem processes and uses simple models in R.
y3-statistics: Both teach experimental design and multivariable/generalised models, categorical outcomes, assumptions and R analysis. UCR examples concern health and behaviour rather than the full range of biological research.
y1-environmental-biology: Both examine human impacts on species, habitats and biological communities and the scientific basis of nature protection. UCR focuses on biodiversity loss and conservation planning rather than the whole environmental-biology field.
y1-science-communication: Both develop communication of biological research to a wider public. UCR’s substantial marine-biology outreach project supplies this shared educational function; Leiden has a dedicated course analysing communication forms and producing a popular-science article.

audience.programmeDescription: Biology at Leiden studies living systems from molecules and cells to organisms, evolution and ecosystems. This comparison follows the broad Biology specialisation, with substantial laboratory, quantitative and research training.
audience.comparisonExplanation: The UCR programmes offer three biological emphases: a broad combination, molecular and biomedical biology with computational methods, or ecology and environmental change. Leiden provides more dedicated plant, developmental and systems biology, a structured Biology elective programme and a required full-time research project. The UCR methods and laboratory courses do not imply completion of that project.

curriculum.limitation: The pathway totals 180 EC: 60 EC in year one; 30 EC of compulsory study and 30 EC of restricted Biology choices in year two; and 30 EC of open study, 6 EC of methods and academic skills, and a 24-EC research project in year three. Biology choices follow five teaching blocks. Their possible subjects are choices, not compulsory additions.

componentNotes.y2-biology-profiling: 30 EC chosen from the Biology elective list across five blocks of four to five weeks. Select one available option per block; the list includes molecular, microbial, organismal and ecological subjects and field research.
componentNotes.y3-bachelor-project: Required 24-EC project, normally 1 March to 2 July 2027: 90 full-time working days. All first-year courses must be passed. Projects normally use a Leiden biological or affiliated institute; external projects require discussion with the study adviser and examination-board approval. Students may work in pairs but write individual English reports. September starts require an approved adjusted study plan.
componentNotes.y3-general-research-skills: Required 2-EC research-skills course, with assignments during the research project. September participation requires an approved adjusted study plan.
componentNotes.y3-statistics: Required 3-EC Statistics 2, normally completed in February before the research project begins. September participation is restricted to approved adjusted plans or a resit.
componentNotes.y3-elective-space: 30 EC in the first semester for a minor, exchange or self-chosen approved course package.
